# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The rapid expansion of transcatheter therapies for structural heart disease has created an increasing demand for large-bore vascular access in patients who are frequently elderly and burdened with peripheral arterial disease. Transfemoral access remains the default for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), but up to 15% of candidates have iliofemoral anatomy unsuitable for large-bore delivery systems [1,2]. Alternative access routes—transapical, transaortic, subclavian/axillary, transcarotid, and transcaval—have therefore been developed [3,4]. Among these, transcaval access has emerged as a fully percutaneous, non-thoracic option that exploits the proximity of the inferior vena cava (IVC) to the abdominal aorta [5].

## Concept and Rationale

Transcaval access involves crossing from the IVC into the abdominal aorta through an electrified guidewire, advancing a delivery sheath across this iatrogenic aorto-caval tract, and closing the aortic access site with a nitinol occluder at the conclusion of the procedure [5,6]. The technique was pioneered at the National Institutes of Health, where preclinical work demonstrated that the retroperitoneum can tamponade bleeding and that the pressure gradient favoring flow from aorta to the lower-pressure cava limits catastrophic hemorrhage [6,7]. The first-in-human series, published in 2014, established procedural feasibility for TAVR and endovascular aortic procedures [8].

## Technique

Preprocedural multidetector computed tomography is essential for planning, identifying a calcium-free target on the aortic wall and an apposed segment of IVC, typically between the renal arteries and the aortic bifurcation [9,10]. A target snare or a stiff wire placed from the contralateral femoral artery may serve as a fluoroscopic radio-opaque marker [10]. Crossing is achieved by directing an electrified 0.014-inch guidewire, energized with electrocautery, from a directional catheter in the IVC toward the aortic target [5,11]. Once the wire is snared in the aorta, the tract is dilated and the large-bore sheath advanced [11]. After completion of the valve or device implantation, the aortotomy is closed using a nitinol duct occluder, with residual flow generally decompressing into the cava [12].

## Clinical Outcomes

The prospective multicenter Transcaval Access for TAVR study enrolled 100 patients with no other good access option and reported a procedural success rate of 99%, with successful caval closure in 98% [13]. Although clinically significant bleeding and vascular complications occurred, mortality and outcomes were favorable given the prohibitive-access population [13,14]. Subsequent registries and single-center experiences have confirmed reproducibility, with transcaval TAVR yielding outcomes comparable to other alternative-access approaches and, in some analyses, superior to transapical and transaortic routes owing to its avoidance of thoracotomy and general anesthesia in many cases [15,16,17]. Importantly, residual aorto-caval fistulae frequently persist but are typically small, hemodynamically inconsequential, and often close spontaneously over time [18,19].

## Comparison with Other Access Routes

Comparative studies suggest that non-transfemoral access is associated with worse outcomes than transfemoral TAVR overall, but transcaval access compares favorably within the alternative-access category [20,21]. The avoidance of chest wall trauma facilitates earlier mobilization and may reduce respiratory complications relative to transapical and direct aortic approaches [22,23]. Transcarotid and transaxillary access are increasingly used and offer comparable results, but transcaval remains valuable when the great vessels are also diseased or unsuitable [24,25]. The choice among alternatives should be individualized through a multidisciplinary heart team evaluation [26].

## Complications and Limitations

The principal concerns are retroperitoneal and intraperitoneal bleeding, which can occur when the crossing or closure site is not fully tamponaded by retroperitoneal tissue [13,27]. Careful CT planning to select an infrarenal target where the aorta and cava are directly apposed minimizes this risk [9,27]. Other complications include device embolization, arteriovenous fistula with high-output features (rare), and access-site vascular injury [28]. The technique demands operator experience and specialized equipment, and outcomes improve along a learning curve [29]. Dedicated closure devices designed specifically for transcaval applications are under investigation and may further enhance safety [30].

## Conclusion

Transcaval access is an established, fully percutaneous strategy that expands transcatheter therapy to patients lacking suitable transfemoral or alternative arterial access. With careful CT-based planning, electrified guidewire crossing, and nitinol occluder closure, it offers high procedural success and acceptable safety in an inherently high-risk population. Ongoing refinement of dedicated closure technology and accumulating registry data will continue to define its optimal role within the structural heart armamentarium [13,30].
